keyVerseText: In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it;
rootMeaning: The name סַרְגּוֹן (Çargôwn) is of foreign derivation and likely originates from the Assyrian Šargânu or Šarrukênu, which can be understood as 'prince of the sun' or a title implying firmness, faithfulness, and kingship. This etymological background highlights a royal and divine association, suggesting not only political authority but a symbolic connection to the sun as a source of power and legitimacy. Thus, the literal sense adds a layer of meaning beyond the English gloss 'Sargon,' emphasizing his role as a divinely endorsed ruler.
usageInScripture: The word סַרְגּוֹן appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Isaiah 20:1, where it is translated as 'when Sargon.' This singular occurrence reflects a precise historical reference to the Assyrian king known for his military campaigns, particularly the conquest of Samaria. The consistency of this translation underscores the importance of identifying this figure as a concrete historical agent within God's unfolding plan, rather than a generic title.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding סַרְגּוֹן as a name meaning 'prince of the sun' and its historical role as an Assyrian king enriches our grasp of God's sovereignty over nations and rulers. Sargon’s identity as a conqueror used in Isaiah’s prophecy reminds believers that earthly powers, even those opposing God's people, serve within His divine providence. This perspective encourages trust in God's ultimate control, affirming that even formidable empires fulfill His purposes in history. It also points forward to the supremacy of Christ, the true King whose reign surpasses all earthly dominions.
keyVerseReflection: Isaiah 20:1 states, 'In the year that Tartan came unto Ashdod, (when Sargon the king of Assyria sent him,) and fought against Ashdod, and took it;' highlighting Sargon’s role as the initiator of Assyrian military action. The mention of Sargon grounds the prophecy in a specific historical context, showing God’s awareness and sovereignty over the events involving powerful foreign kings. The name סַרְגּוֹן here signals the reality of God’s interaction with history through known rulers, affirming His control even over those who oppose His people.
